html:
The building material of ancient Rome: lime mortar mixed with broken stone or brick, in Latin opus caementicium. In use from about the 2nd century BCE, it let the Romans build vaults, domes and harbours on a scale no one had managed before.

The key was volcanic ash from around Puteoli, near Naples, called pozzolana. Mixed with lime it set hard even under water. Vitruvius describes it. Roman builders poured concrete into forms and usually faced it with brick or stone, so it rarely shows on the surface.

It made possible:

  • great vaulted halls and baths;
  • the dome of the Pantheon, still the largest dome of unreinforced concrete in the world;
  • the foundations and vaults of the Colosseum;
  • harbour moles built out into the sea, as at Portus.

Many Roman concrete structures still stand after two thousand years. Studies suggest lumps of lime in the mix helped small cracks seal themselves. The skill faded after the Roman Empire fell in the west, and builders did not match its domes for many centuries.
